newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Bayer unit fined $50 million for price fixing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Bayer unit fined $50 million for price fixing.

text.p: A U.S. subsidiary of the German chemical giant Bayer AG was sentenced to a $50 million fine on Wednesday after pleading guilty to taking part in an international conspiracy to fix citric acid prices.

U.S. District Judge Fern Smith handed down the sentence in San Francisco after accepting a plea agreement between New Jersey-based Haarmann & Reimer Corp and the U.S. Justice Department announced earlier in Washington.

She also sentenced Hans Hartmann, a senior executive at Haarmann & Reimer's German counterpart, to a $150,000 fine after he pleaded guilty to taking part in the conspiracy. Hartmann, a 62-year-old German citizen, was not sentenced to any jail time.

The Haarmann & Reimer fine was the second largest criminal antitrust fine after the $100 million fine against Archer Daniels Midland Co, the agricultural products giant, which pleaded guilty to taking part in conspiracies involving two additives last October.

"This $50 million criminal fine is a clear message to corporations around the world," Attorney General Janet Reno said. "We will not tolerate international conspiracies that defraud American consumers."
Citric acid is a flavor additive and preservative found in soft drinks, processed food, detergents and pharmaceutical products. It is a $1.2 billion a year industry worldwide.

Smith set a five-year schedule for Haarmann & Reimer to pay the $50 million fine. The first $10 million must be paid within 30 days and the remaining $40 million in five annual instalments of $8 million starting one year from now.

The one-count felony charge alleged that Haarmann & Reimer, through several of its employees, conspired with other unidentified major citric acid-producing firms to suppress and eliminate competition from July 1991 to June 1995.

The charge said the conspirators took part in meetings at which they agreed to set citric acid prices at certain levels and agreed on the volume of citric acid that each company would sell in the United States and elsewhere.

Justice Department officials allege that a group of senior executives known as the "the Masters" came up with the general plans while the details were worked out by a lower group of managers known as "Sherpas."
The conspirators shared sales volume figures and companies that sold too much had to buy citric acid from the other conspirators in the following year, the officials said.

The investigation dates back to 1992 and grew out of an initial probe of Archer Daniels Midland Co. Acting Assistant Attorney General Joel Klein said the investigation remains active in the United States, Europe and Asia.

In an earlier civil case, Haarmann & Reimer, Archer Daniels, Hoffman-LaRoche Inc., a subsidiary of Roche Holding, and the Austrian-based Jungbunzlauer Inc. in December agreed to settle a price-fixing lawsuit.
The companies agreed to pay a total of $94 million to settle the class-action lawsuit filed by food processors in California. A fifth defendant, Cargill Inc., did not join the settlement.
Justice Department officials declined to name any of the other companies now under investigation.

As part of the plea deal, the Justice Department agreed to bring no further prosecutions against Haarmann & Reimer or against any other executives or employees who cooperate in the probe, the officials said.

In return, the company agreed to turn over documents and make its current and former officers, directors and employees available for questioning and possible testimony before grand juries or trials, at the firm's expense, they said.
